young.html: In a village in La Mancha, in the middle of Spain, lived a thin, gray-haired gentleman who loved to read. His favorite books were about knights: brave heroes who rode out to fight giants, rescue princesses and defeat wicked enchanters. He read so many that he began to believe every word.

One day he put on his great-grandfather's rusty armor, named his bony old horse Rocinante, chose a farm girl he had hardly met as his lady (he called her Dulcinea), named himself Don Quixote of La Mancha, and rode out to be a knight. Soon he talked a round, practical farmer named Sancho Panza into riding with him as his squire, on a donkey.
Everywhere they go, Don Quixote sees adventure. An inn becomes a castle. A flock of sheep becomes an army. And one morning, on the windy plain, he sees thirty or forty giants waving their arms...

full.html: Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616) lived a life as full of adventure as any romance. He was wounded at the great sea battle of Lepanto (1571) and lost the use of his left hand; he was captured by pirates and held in Algiers for five years, trying four times to escape; back in Spain he worked as a tax collector and was jailed over his accounts. In his late fifties he published The Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha (1605). It was a hit at once.

The book began as a parody of the romances of chivalry, long tales of knights such as Amadis of Gaul, which were wildly popular in Spain. In Chapter VI the village priest and barber hold a comic trial of Don Quixote's library and burn most of it, sparing the books they think good. But the story grew into something much larger: a long conversation between a dreamer and a realist, and a portrait of all of Spain on the road.

full.text:
"Fortune is arranging matters for us better than we could have shaped our desires ourselves, for look there, friend Sancho Panza, where thirty or more monstrous giants present themselves, all of whom I mean to engage in battle and slay, and with whose spoils we shall begin to make our fortunes; for this is righteous warfare, and it is God's good service to sweep so evil a breed from off the face of the earth."

"What giants?" said Sancho Panza.
full.author: Cervantes
full.work: Don Quixote, Part One, Chapter VIII

full.text: "Look, your worship," said Sancho; "what we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that turned by the wind make the millstone go."
full.author: Cervantes
full.work: Don Quixote, Part One, Chapter VIII

full.html: Don Quixote charges anyway. A sail catches his lance and sends horse and rider tumbling. His explanation: an enchanter must have turned the giants into windmills to rob him of the glory. That pattern, a vision, a collision with reality, and a new story to save the vision, repeats through the book.

full.html: Sancho Panza joins for the promise of an island to govern. He is earthy, fond of food and sleep, full of proverbs, and often wiser than his master about the world; Don Quixote is learned, brave, courteous, and wrong about almost everything he sees. Over the book each rubs off on the other: Sancho starts to dream, and Don Quixote starts to doubt. Their talk on the road is the heart of the novel.

Part One is also a collection: shepherds' love stories, a tale read aloud at an inn ("The Ill-Advised Curiosity"), and the story of a captive escaped from Algiers that echoes Cervantes's own. In Chapter IX the narrator claims he found the rest of the history in Arabic notebooks by one Cide Hamete Benengeli, a joke about storytellers that grows in Part Two.

Many critics call Don Quixote the first modern novel: a long prose story about ordinary life, told with irony, in which characters change. It was translated into English by Thomas Shelton as early as 1612; John Ormsby's translation (1885) is the one quoted here. The words quixotic (nobly but impractically idealistic) and "tilting at windmills" come from it.

Thinking Don Quixote is only a joke at the knight's expense. Cervantes laughs at him, but also lets him be generous, brave and right about some things that matter: honor, kindness, the dignity of a promise. Readers have argued ever since whether he is a fool, a hero or both.

deep.html: Don Quixote goes mad from reading, and lives as if life were a book. Every reader of this ladder might ask: how do the books we read shape what we see? In Dante's Inferno, earlier, two lovers say a book about Lancelot led them astray (Canto V); Flaubert's Madame Bovary, later in literature, is another reader undone by romances.

items: Is it better to see the world as it is, like Sancho, or as it ought to be, like Don Quixote?

Why does a story about a failed knight still move readers four hundred years later?

questions: Have you ever imagined something so hard that you almost believed it? What happened?
Would you rather travel with Don Quixote or with Sancho? Why?
Don Quixote wants to help people, but often makes things worse. Do good intentions matter if the results are bad?
Why do you think people today call a hopeless but noble cause "tilting at windmills"?
